禮記
凡侍坐於大司成者，遠近間三席，可以問；終則負墻，列事未盡不問。
獨樂其志，不厭其道；備舉其道，不私其欲。是故情見而義立，樂終而德尊。
盡其道，端其義，而教生焉。
獻君，君舉旅，行酬而后獻卿；卿舉旅，行酬一而后獻大夫；大夫舉旅，行酬而后獻士；士舉旅，行酬而后獻庶子。

第貳場
論
脩身則道立。

詔誥表內科一道。
擬漢親耕籍田詔，文帝二年。
擬唐以長孫無忌為右僕射誥，貞觀元年。
擬宋起太師文彦博平章軍國重事班宰相上謝表，元祐元年。
translation_en:
…[Zhong]sun Heji and the Viscount of Zhu made a covenant at Gouyi. Second year of Duke Ai.

Record of Rites
Whenever seated in attendance upon the Grand Director of Education, one should leave an interval of three mats, whether nearer or farther away, and may ask questions. When finished, one withdraws to the wall. Until the matters being presented have been exhausted, one does not ask questions.
He alone takes delight in his aspirations and never tires of his Way; he fully puts his Way into practice and does not selfishly pursue his desires. Thus his feelings become manifest and righteousness is established; when the music ends, his virtue is held in reverence.
Fully realize its Way and set its moral principles aright, and teaching arises from this.
An offering of wine is made to the ruler. The ruler initiates the general circulation of cups; after the exchange of toasts, wine is offered to the ministers. The ministers initiate the general circulation of cups; after one round of exchanged toasts, wine is offered to the grandees. The grandees initiate the general circulation of cups; after the exchange of toasts, wine is offered to the officers. The officers initiate the general circulation of cups; after the exchange of toasts, wine is offered to the younger sons.

Second Session
Discourse
Through cultivating oneself, the Way is established.

One topic from among edicts, proclamations, and memorials [?].
Compose an edict in the voice of the Han emperor on personally plowing the imperial field. Second year of Emperor Wen.
Compose a proclamation in the voice of the Tang emperor appointing Zhangsun Wuji as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs. First year of Zhenguan.
Compose a memorial of thanks in the voice of Wen Yanbo of the Song upon his recall as Grand Preceptor to deliberate on important military and state affairs, with precedence above the chief councilors. First year of Yuanyou.

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
判語〔五條〕
舉用有過官吏
錢粮互相覺察
見任官輒自立碑
私越冒度関津
詐教誘人犯法
第叁場
第五道
問古昔帝王之有天下必制度以飭治功
===
脩典章以詔後世我
國家
祖宗列聖
御製諸書布之天下固已家傳人誦雖文身左
衽之國罔不祗若而尊信之頃者
孝宗敬皇帝仰承
英廟之志復有會典之作我
皇上繼述益勤命儒臣讐校而頒布焉凡百五
十年之間沿革損益之政無乎不具
punctuated:
判語〔五條〕
舉用有過官吏。
錢粮互相覺察。
見任官輒自立碑。
私越冒度関津。
詐教誘人犯法。

第叁場
第五道
問：古昔帝王之有天下，必制度以飭治功，脩典章以詔後世。我國家祖宗列聖御製諸書，布之天下，固已家傳人誦；雖文身左衽之國，罔不祗若而尊信之。頃者，孝宗敬皇帝仰承英廟之志，復有會典之作。我皇上繼述益勤，命儒臣讐校而頒布焉。凡百五十年之間沿革損益之政，無乎不具。
translation_en:
Legal judgments 〔five items〕
Recommending and appointing officials and clerks with prior offenses.
Mutual scrutiny of matters concerning money and grain.
Serving officials erecting commemorative steles for themselves without authorization.
Clandestinely crossing or fraudulently passing through checkpoints and ferries.
Deceitfully instructing or enticing others to violate the law.

Third Session
Fifth Question
Question: When the emperors and kings of antiquity possessed All-under-Heaven, they invariably established institutions to put the work of government in order and revised statutes and regulations to instruct later generations. The books imperially composed by the successive sage rulers, the ancestors of our dynasty, have been distributed throughout the realm; indeed, they have already been handed down in every household and recited by everyone. Even among countries whose people tattoo their bodies and fasten their garments on the left, none fail reverently to comply with them and to esteem and trust them. Recently, Emperor Xiaozong, posthumously honored as Jing, reverently carried forward the intentions of Emperor Yingzong and further undertook the compilation of the Collected Statutes (Huidian). Our present emperor, ever more diligent in continuing their work, ordered his scholarly officials to collate and revise it and then promulgated it. It comprehensively records all the measures retained, changed, curtailed, or expanded over the course of a hundred and fifty years.

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
今士大夫得覩
宸編若獲拱璧私家之蔵永爲世寶不知是典
近何所稽遠何所取而
制作之本意可仰窺而測識之邪夫有典有則
貽厥子孫
先帝爲後世慮至深遠也今日臣工敬而誦之
體而行之不知其要何在諸生幸以
其所知者告我
一問人君之治天下非賞無以慶善非罰
===
無以威惡固也然酬酢運用之間少戾
其常則不免於過中失正之弊均賞矣
而不足以爲勸均罰矣而不足以爲懲
是果何說哉古之人有懼殃民而不許
求郎之請者有念至公而不私秦府舊
人者又有因太原未平而不與使相者
賞善如是無乃吝之過而近於刻印刓
忍弗予者乎有因上書而除肉刑者有
念不能全民之生而再定笞令者又有
punctuated:
今士大夫得覩宸編，若獲拱璧，私家之蔵，永爲世寶。不知是典，近何所稽，遠何所取，而制作之本意可仰窺而測識之邪？夫有典有則，貽厥子孫，先帝爲後世慮至深遠也。今日臣工敬而誦之，體而行之，不知其要何在？諸生幸以其所知者告我。
一問：人君之治天下，非賞無以慶善，非罰無以威惡，固也。然酬酢運用之間，少戾其常，則不免於過中失正之弊。均賞矣，而不足以爲勸；均罰矣，而不足以爲懲。是果何說哉？古之人，有懼殃民而不許求郎之請者，有念至公而不私秦府舊人者，又有因太原未平而不與使相者。賞善如是，無乃吝之過，而近於刻印刓，忍弗予者乎？有因上書而除肉刑者，有念不能全民之生而再定笞令者，又有
translation_en:
Now that scholar-officials can behold this imperial compilation, they prize it as though they had obtained a jade disk held in both hands; preserved in private collections, it will forever be a treasure handed down through the generations. Yet what precedents from recent times does this compendium consult, and what does it draw upon from the distant past? Can we reverently discern and comprehend the original intention behind its compilation? Indeed, “There are statutes and there are rules, bequeathed to their descendants”: the late emperor’s concern for later generations was exceedingly profound and far-reaching. Today officials respectfully recite it and put it into practice, but where does its essential import lie? Students, kindly tell me what you know.
One question: In governing all under Heaven, a ruler cannot honor goodness without rewards or deter evil without punishments. This is certainly so. Yet in responding to affairs and applying these measures, the slightest departure from their proper norms inevitably leads to the faults of exceeding the mean and losing what is right. Rewards may alike be bestowed, yet fail to encourage; punishments may alike be imposed, yet fail to deter. How, indeed, is this to be explained? Among rulers of antiquity, one feared bringing calamity upon the people and therefore refused a request for appointment as a Court Gentleman; another, mindful of absolute impartiality, showed no favoritism toward former members of the Prince of Qin’s establishment; and another withheld appointment as Military Commissioner with a concurrent grand councilor title because Taiyuan had not yet been pacified. In rewarding goodness in this way, were they not excessively parsimonious, approaching the conduct of one who had a seal engraved but wore it smooth through handling, bringing himself to withhold it? There was one who abolished mutilating punishments in response to a written petition; another, concerned that he could not preserve the people’s lives, revised the regulations for beating with the light stick a second time; and there was also one who…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
讀明堂鍼灸書而禁鞭背者恤刑如是
無乃畏之過而近於斷死刑垂涕泣者
乎茲欲一賞而人無不勸一怒而人無不
威其要安在考之論刑賞者說亦不一
或曰善為國者賞不僭而刑不濫又曰
寧僭無濫矣何仕者復有世祿之制刑
國復有重典之施歟或曰為政者不賞
私勞不罰私怨是矣何孔門問答復有
以直報怨以德報德之說將舊有德怨
===
之人待之不能不異歟或者又曰有功
不賞有罪不刑雖唐虞不能以化天下
而與不賞而民勸不怒而民威於鈇鉞
者何背馳也或者又曰有功則賞有罪
則刑雖敢不竭心盡力以脩職業而宋
臣又謂有功而後爵天下必有遺善故
有無功而爵者有罪而後罰天下必有
遺惡故有無罪而罰者斯二說者又何
如其抵捂也諸生明經待問久矣於是
punctuated: 讀明堂鍼灸書而禁鞭背者。恤刑如是，無乃畏之過而近於斷死刑垂涕泣者乎？茲欲一賞而人無不勸，一怒而人無不威，其要安在？考之論刑賞者，說亦不一。或曰：「善為國者，賞不僭而刑不濫。」又曰：「寧僭無濫。」矣，何仕者復有世祿之制，刑國復有重典之施歟？或曰：「為政者，不賞私勞，不罰私怨。」是矣，何孔門問答復有「以直報怨，以德報德」之說？將舊有德怨之人，待之不能不異歟？或者又曰：「有功不賞，有罪不刑，雖唐虞不能以化天下。」而與「不賞而民勸，不怒而民威於鈇鉞」者，何背馳也？或者又曰：「有功則賞，有罪則刑，雖敢不竭心盡力以脩職業？」而宋臣又謂：「有功而後爵，天下必有遺善，故有無功而爵者；有罪而後罰，天下必有遺惡，故有無罪而罰者。」斯二說者，又何如其抵捂也？諸生明經待問久矣，於是
translation_en:
…those who, after reading the Mingtang Book of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, prohibited flogging the back. With such concern over punishments, were they not excessively apprehensive, approaching the conduct of those who shed tears when pronouncing a death sentence? Now, if we wish a single reward to encourage everyone, and a single display of anger to inspire awe in everyone, where does the essential principle lie?

Examining discussions of punishments and rewards, we find that the explanations also differ. Some say, “Those skilled at governing a state do not bestow undeserved rewards or impose excessive punishments.” They also say, “Better to bestow undeserved rewards than to impose excessive punishments.” Why, then, was there also a system of hereditary stipends for those in office, and why were severe penal codes also applied in governing states? Some say, “Those who govern do not reward services rendered to them privately or punish private grievances.” This is correct; yet why do the questions and answers in the school of Confucius also contain the saying, “Repay resentment with uprightness, and kindness with kindness”? Does this mean that one cannot help treating differently those from whom one has previously received kindness or suffered injury?

Others say, “If merit goes unrewarded and crime unpunished, even the rulers of Tang and Yu could not transform the realm.” Why does this run counter to the saying, “Without rewards the people are encouraged; without anger the people stand in greater awe than before executioners’ axes”? Others again say, “If merit is rewarded and crime punished, who would dare [?] not devote all his heart and strength to discharging his official duties?” Yet a minister of the Song also stated, “If noble rank is conferred only after meritorious service, some goodness in the realm will inevitably go unrecognized; hence some receive rank without meritorious service. If punishment is imposed only after a crime, some evil in the realm will inevitably escape; hence some are punished without having committed a crime.” How is it that these two explanations likewise contradict one another? You students have long studied the Classics and awaited questioning. Concerning these…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
二事與前數說相與質而訂之何如
問風俗教化儒先論之詳矣教化本於朝
廷而責任於守令風俗移于好尚而振
作于士人固史以來所傳循吏非一然
觀其所稱者不曰力行教化則曰教以
禮讓可舉其人而言之歟今之為守令
者以因循苟免為賢嚴急集事為能至
於古之教化槩乎其未聞也其故何哉
又嘗觀乎古人之有意於風俗者其嘉
===
言善行誠可師法故有誤認車牛而不
與較者有苦居畎畝而不入城府者有
歸亡父之金而不肯受者有遜其園為
黌舍者有退居于洛而不言時事者之
數者非甚高遠而難能也今有之不亦
可以興廉而崇讓乎有為無不是父母
之說者有為難得兄弟之說者有為絕
交令可交出妻令可嫁之說者有為居
是邦不非其大夫之說者又有為律設
punctuated:
二事與前數說，相與質而訂之，何如？
問：風俗教化，儒先論之詳矣。教化本於朝廷，而責任於守令；風俗移于好尚，而振作于士人。固史以來所傳循吏非一，然觀其所稱者，不曰力行教化，則曰教以禮讓。可舉其人而言之歟？今之為守令者，以因循苟免為賢，嚴急集事為能，至於古之教化，槩乎其未聞也。其故何哉？又嘗觀乎古人之有意於風俗者，其嘉言善行，誠可師法。故有誤認車牛而不與較者，有苦居畎畝而不入城府者，有歸亡父之金而不肯受者，有遜其園為黌舍者，有退居于洛而不言時事者。之數者非甚高遠而難能也，今有之，不亦可以興廉而崇讓乎？有為無不是父母之說者，有為難得兄弟之說者，有為絕交令可交、出妻令可嫁之說者，有為居是邦不非其大夫之說者，又有為律設
translation_en:
…these two matters together with the several preceding views: how would you examine and adjudicate them in discussion with one another?
Question: Earlier Confucian scholars discussed customs and moral transformation in detail. Moral transformation originates at court, while responsibility for it rests with prefects and district magistrates; customs shift with prevailing preferences, while their renewal depends upon scholars. The historical records [?] have transmitted accounts of many exemplary officials. Yet when we examine the praise they received, it speaks either of their strenuous practice of moral instruction or of their teaching through ritual propriety and deference. Can you name these men and discuss them? Those who serve as prefects and district magistrates today regard following established routines and merely escaping blame as worthiness, and harsh urgency in accomplishing business as ability. As for the moral instruction of antiquity, they seem never to have heard of it. Why is this?
I have also considered men of antiquity who took an interest in customs. Their admirable words and good deeds truly deserve emulation. Thus, there was one who did not dispute with someone who mistakenly claimed his cart and ox; one who endured hardship living among the fields and did not enter the city or government offices; one who refused to accept gold returned as belonging to his deceased father [?]; one who yielded his garden for a school; and one who retired to Luo and did not discuss current affairs. These examples are neither excessively lofty nor difficult to accomplish. If such conduct existed today, could it not encourage integrity and esteem for deference? Some advanced the saying that no parents are ever in the wrong; some, that brothers are hard to come by; some, that when severing a friendship one should leave room for its renewal, and when dismissing a wife one should leave her able to remarry; some, that when living in a state one should not condemn its great officers. There were also those who said that statutes establish…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
大法禮順人情之說者是数者亦非空
言而無施也今信而行之不猶可以寛
鄙而敦薄乎夫禮義廉耻謂之四維四
維之張弛其所係大矣吾爲此懼而相
與折衷冀有聞焉幸毋迂以視我
問西漢尚寛大東漢尚節義史氏之論尚
矣今以西漢之人物考之有不受卒徒
𠼪背者有不聽兩吏挾持者有見大將
軍而不拜者有至虜庭而不屈者上欲
===
起禮樂也徵之而不肯行上方興文學
也答以不在多言由是觀之西漢之節
義何歉於東漢哉夫兩漢之節義信皆
有之矣而先儒又有爲東漢節義不如
西漢之說者是果然歟否歟迨至于唐
有死守江淮者有伏閤極諫者有布衣
對策極言時政者有太學儒生倡義止
亂者宋之時又有使虜庭而抗論者有
年彊仕而勇退者有被謫雖困而無書
punctuated:
大法，禮順人情之說者。是数者亦非空言而無施也。今信而行之，不猶可以寛鄙而敦薄乎？夫禮義廉耻，謂之四維。四維之張弛，其所係大矣。吾爲此懼，而相與折衷，冀有聞焉。幸毋迂以視我。

問：西漢尚寛大，東漢尚節義，史氏之論尚矣。今以西漢之人物考之，有不受卒徒𠼪背者，有不聽兩吏挾持者，有見大將軍而不拜者，有至虜庭而不屈者。上欲起禮樂也，徵之而不肯行；上方興文學也，答以不在多言。由是觀之，西漢之節義何歉於東漢哉？夫兩漢之節義，信皆有之矣，而先儒又有爲東漢節義不如西漢之說者，是果然歟，否歟？迨至于唐，有死守江淮者，有伏閤極諫者，有布衣對策極言時政者，有太學儒生倡義止亂者。宋之時，又有使虜庭而抗論者，有年彊仕而勇退者，有被謫雖困而無書
translation_en:
…broad rules, while ritual accords with human feelings. These several teachings, too, are no empty words without practical application. If today we trust and practice them, could we not likewise broaden narrow minds and give substance to shallow character? Ritual propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame are called the Four Bonds. Whether these bonds are taut or slack has momentous consequences. Apprehensive about this, I seek together with you to arrive at a balanced judgment, hoping to learn something. Please do not regard me as impractical.

Question: The Western Han esteemed magnanimity, and the Eastern Han esteemed moral integrity and righteousness: this judgment of the historians is long established. Yet if we examine the figures of the Western Han, there were those who would not tolerate soldiers spitting on their backs [?], those who would not allow two functionaries to hold them on either side, those who would not bow when meeting the General-in-Chief, and those who reached the court of the northern enemies but would not submit. When the emperor wished to revive rites and music, one man refused to go when summoned; when the emperor was promoting literary learning, another replied that it did not consist in an abundance of words. Viewed in this light, how was the moral integrity and righteousness of the Western Han inferior to that of the Eastern Han? Both Han dynasties certainly possessed these qualities. Yet earlier Confucian scholars also maintained that the Eastern Han fell short of the Western Han in moral integrity and righteousness. Was this really so, or not?

Coming down to the Tang, there were those who defended the Jiang–Huai region to the death, those who prostrated themselves at the palace gate and remonstrated with utmost force, those who, as commoners, answered policy questions and spoke with complete frankness about contemporary government, and students of the Imperial University who rallied support for a righteous cause and halted disorder. In the Song, too, there were those who went as envoys to the enemy court and argued without yielding, those who resolutely retired at forty—the age for entering official service—and those who, though impoverished in banishment, sent no letters…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
至京師者有交游雖舊而無書抵政府
者唐宋之節義如是又何歉於兩漢哉
然後世之論獨以節義歸之於東漢者
其故安在而史氏之言去漢未遠果不
足信否歟是必有攸當之說請明言之
且以觀平居之所養
問今日之務所重而可議者莫切於食與
兵蓋非兵無以禦侮非食無以供費古
者藏兵於民而兵足用田不加賦而食
===
足供固無庸議矣厥後創業如漢高提
兵恒數十萬以一蕭何餽餉而有餘守
成如文帝遣四將軍以禦匈奴其兵亦
已衆矣然屢蠲田租或詔減半而國用
不聞告竭不知當時何以能然也今兵
掌於司馬督於憲臣簡閱之法清理之
規未嘗廢也但四方諸路之兵不足以
制諸路之寇卒遇有警至勤
王師或募土兵或調邊將噫我兵之弱何至
punctuated:
至京師者，有交游雖舊而無書抵政府者。唐宋之節義如是，又何歉於兩漢哉？然後世之論，獨以節義歸之於東漢者，其故安在？而史氏之言，去漢未遠，果不足信否歟？是必有攸當之說，請明言之，且以觀平居之所養。
問：今日之務，所重而可議者，莫切於食與兵。蓋非兵無以禦侮，非食無以供費。古者藏兵於民，而兵足用；田不加賦，而食足供，固無庸議矣。厥後創業如漢高，提兵恒數十萬，以一蕭何餽餉而有餘；守成如文帝，遣四將軍以禦匈奴，其兵亦已衆矣。然屢蠲田租，或詔減半，而國用不聞告竭。不知當時何以能然也？今兵掌於司馬，督於憲臣，簡閱之法、清理之規，未嘗廢也。但四方諸路之兵，不足以制諸路之寇，卒遇有警，至勤王師，或募土兵，或調邊將。噫！我兵之弱，何至
translation_en:
…reached the capital; others, though their friendships were longstanding, sent no letters to those in government. Such was the moral integrity of the Tang and Song. How, then, was it in any way inferior to that of the Western and Eastern Han? Yet later discussions attribute moral integrity exclusively to the Eastern Han. Why is this? And are the words of historians who lived not long after the Han truly unworthy of belief? There must surely be an explanation that properly addresses this. Please state it clearly, so that we may also see what you have cultivated in your everyday life.
Question: Among the important affairs of the present day that warrant discussion, none is more pressing than provisions and troops. Without troops there is no means of resisting aggression; without provisions there is no means of meeting expenses. In antiquity, soldiers were maintained among the common people, and there were sufficient troops for service; no additional taxes were imposed on the fields, yet provisions were sufficient. This certainly requires no debate. Later, a founder such as Gaozu of Han regularly commanded several hundred thousand troops, yet with Xiao He alone supplying them, there was more than enough. A ruler preserving an established dynasty, such as Emperor Wen, dispatched four generals to resist the Xiongnu, and his troops too were numerous. Yet he repeatedly remitted the land tax, sometimes ordering it reduced by half, and there were no reports that state resources were exhausted. How was this possible at the time? Today, troops are administered by the Minister of War and supervised by censorial officials. The procedures for mustering and inspecting them and the regulations for reviewing and rectifying their rolls have never been abandoned. Yet the troops in the various regions throughout the realm cannot subdue the bandits in those regions. When an emergency suddenly arises, it becomes necessary to call upon the imperial army, sometimes recruiting local troops and sometimes transferring frontier commanders. Alas! How has the weakness of our troops reached…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
是哉兵食之供掌於司徒綱於藩司其
征輸之法儲峙之規未少變也但各省
一歲之積不足以供一歲之費一有所
需則束手無策非請
內帑則截綱運矣噫我財之匱何至是哉豈
典兵理財者未得其人將兵之訓練者
未精而逃亡者未盡復伍歟冗食之員
尚多而無益之費未盡裁省歟抑別有
其故也或者曰邇年盜賊動以千萬非
===
區區尋常兵力之可勝而天下府庫之
空虛民力之重困又非一朝一夕可以
完復而捄藥者宜大有所處不知其計
將安出願明言之
punctuated: 是哉？兵食之供，掌於司徒，綱於藩司，其征輸之法、儲峙之規，未少變也。但各省一歲之積，不足以供一歲之費；一有所需，則束手無策，非請內帑，則截綱運矣。噫！我財之匱，何至是哉？豈典兵理財者未得其人，將兵之訓練者未精，而逃亡者未盡復伍歟？冗食之員尚多，而無益之費未盡裁省歟？抑別有其故也？或者曰：「邇年盜賊動以千萬，非區區尋常兵力之可勝，而天下府庫之空虛、民力之重困，又非一朝一夕可以完復，而捄藥者宜大有所處。」不知其計將安出？願明言之。
translation_en:
…to such a pass? Provisioning the troops is under the charge of the Minister of Revenue and coordinated by the Provincial Administration Commissions. The methods of collecting and transporting taxes and the regulations for maintaining reserves have not changed in the slightest. Yet each province’s accumulation for a year is insufficient to meet a year’s expenses. Whenever a need arises, officials are helpless and have no plan: they either request funds from the imperial treasury or divert shipments of tax revenues. Alas! How has the shortage of our resources reached such a pass? Is it that the right men have not been found to manage military affairs and public finance? Or is the troops’ training inadequate, while deserters have not all been restored to the ranks? Are there still too many superfluous personnel drawing sustenance, while useless expenditure has not been fully curtailed? Or is there some other cause?
Some say: “In recent years, bandits have frequently numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands, beyond what meager forces of ordinary strength can overcome. Moreover, the depleted treasuries throughout the realm and the severely exhausted resources of the people cannot be fully restored overnight. Those seeking a remedy must therefore take substantial measures.” What plan, then, can be devised? Please explain it clearly.

First Session

Four Books

“When going out, act as though meeting an honored guest; when employing the people, act as though assisting at a great sacrifice. What you do not desire for yourself, do not impose on others. In service to a state, incur no resentment; in service to a household, incur no resentment.”

Zhao Tingfu

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: 〔Most authors can discuss this subject, but their writing is either stale or merely laudatory [?], making it quite tiresome to read. Suddenly I came upon this script: its phrasing is fresh, yet accords with classical standards. How could one fail to feel respect for it?〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: 〔The Master tells Zhonggong about the practice of benevolence and its results.〕〔His words are plain and concise, yet their savor is inexhaustible. This composition is unforced and restrained, elevated and antique in style, and fully brings out their essential meaning. I imagine that beyond literary accomplishment, its author must possess further learning.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Hao, Instructor: 〔The topic is inherently dignified. Most compositions vie with one another in displays of superficial language. In this composition, the principles expressed exceed the words themselves; I select it.〕

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: 〔He expounds the Sage’s words in solemn language. Surely he understands composition!〕

Comment by Examiner Chen, Professor: 〔The writing flows and the reasoning is coherent: this is beyond the reach of shallow learning.〕

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之人焉有不孚者哉夫子因仲弓問仁而告之
以此謂夫學莫先於爲仁而仁莫切於敬恕是
故敬者德之聚持己不敬則私意有所容於內
非所以爲仁也要必戒慎常存一出門也雖無
大賓是見肅恭收斂儼若接大賓於揖讓之間
罔敢以慢心乘之一使民也雖非大祭是承嚴
恭寅畏恍若承大祭於對越之頃罔敢以易心
處之若然則敬以持己而仁之體立矣恕者仁
之方待物不恕則私意有所容於外亦非所以
爲仁也要必近取諸身以人之心不異於我也
凡我所不欲者則勿以之而施於人待人猶待
己也我之心不殊於人也凡我所不願者則勿
以之而加於彼處己猶處人也若然則恕以及
物而仁之用行矣敬恕兼盡則心德以全由是
外而在邦也自上及下皆相安於敬恕之間欽
仰愛慕而怨惡之不形蓋感應之機自宥不約
而同者焉內而在家也由親及疎咸相承於敬
恕之餘歡欣怡愉而怨讟之不作蓋動物之誠
punctuated: 之人焉有不孚者哉？夫子因仲弓問仁而告之以此，謂夫學莫先於爲仁，而仁莫切於敬恕。是故敬者，德之聚。持己不敬，則私意有所容於內，非所以爲仁也。要必戒慎常存，一出門也，雖無大賓是見，肅恭收斂，儼若接大賓於揖讓之間，罔敢以慢心乘之；一使民也，雖非大祭是承，嚴恭寅畏，恍若承大祭於對越之頃，罔敢以易心處之。若然，則敬以持己，而仁之體立矣。恕者，仁之方。待物不恕，則私意有所容於外，亦非所以爲仁也。要必近取諸身，以人之心不異於我也，凡我所不欲者，則勿以之而施於人，待人猶待己也；我之心不殊於人也，凡我所不願者，則勿以之而加於彼，處己猶處人也。若然，則恕以及物，而仁之用行矣。敬恕兼盡，則心德以全。由是外而在邦也，自上及下，皆相安於敬恕之間，欽仰愛慕，而怨惡之不形，蓋感應之機自宥不約而同者焉；內而在家也，由親及疎，咸相承於敬恕之餘，歡欣怡愉，而怨讟之不作，蓋動物之誠
translation_en: …among these people, how could any fail to respond with trust? When Zhonggong asked about humaneness, the Master instructed him in these terms. He meant that nothing takes precedence in learning over practicing humaneness, and nothing is more essential to humaneness than reverence and reciprocity. Reverence is thus where virtue gathers. If one does not govern oneself with reverence, selfish intentions find room within: this is no way to practice humaneness. One must always remain watchful and cautious. Whenever one goes out, even if no distinguished guest is present, one must be solemn, respectful, and collected, just as though receiving such a guest amid bows and courteous gestures, never daring to let an arrogant disposition intrude. Whenever one employs the people, even if one is not assisting at a great sacrifice, one must be solemn, respectful, vigilant, and awed, as though assisting at such a sacrifice in the presence of the spirits, never daring to approach the task lightly. In this way, reverence governs the self, and the substance of humaneness is established. Reciprocity is the method of humaneness. If one does not deal with others through reciprocity, selfish intentions find room in one’s outward dealings: this too is no way to practice humaneness. One must draw an analogy from what is nearest—oneself. Since others’ hearts do not differ from one’s own, whatever one does not desire oneself must not be imposed on others: treating others is like treating oneself. Since one’s own heart is no different from others’, whatever one does not wish for oneself must not be inflicted upon them: dealing with oneself is like dealing with others. In this way, reciprocity extends to others, and humaneness comes into operation. When reverence and reciprocity are both fully realized, the virtue of the heart is complete. Thus, in the wider sphere of service in a state, those above and below all live at ease with one another amid reverence and reciprocity, feeling respect, admiration, affection, and attachment, without resentment or hatred arising. For the workings of influence and response naturally bring concord without prior agreement [?]. Within the household, from close relations to distant ones, all support one another through the continuing effects of reverence and reciprocity, feeling joy and contentment, without resentment or recrimination arising. For the sincerity that moves others…

text:
自有不戒而孚者焉夫敬恕之功盡而無怨之
效臻仁不外是矣脫效之未臻是功之未至也
雍也盍亦知所自考以為加勉也哉抑仁一也
敬恕之㫖視克復之訓若有弗類何也蓋天之
生物因材而篤聖人教人亦因人而施期於有
成而已雖然一敬可徹於上下而恕亦未可易
而視之也誠能從事於此而有得焉亦將無已
之可克矣
回之為人也擇乎中庸得一善則拳拳服
===
膺而弗失之矣

多則冗短則晦此作發明透徹而又若不竟其說者
豈可多得

膚淺非所以語顏子也此作能槩括其梗槩而探索
其淵微理到而文自工過時輩遠矣

自有不戒而孚者焉。夫敬恕之功盡，而無怨之效臻，仁不外是矣。脫效之未臻，是功之未至也。雍也，盍亦知所自考，以為加勉也哉？抑仁一也，敬恕之㫖視克復之訓，若有弗類，何也？蓋天之生物，因材而篤；聖人教人，亦因人而施，期於有成而已。雖然，一敬可徹於上下，而恕亦未可易而視之也。誠能從事於此而有得焉，亦將無已之可克矣。
回之為人也，擇乎中庸，得一善，則拳拳服膺而弗失之矣。

同考試官教諭戴批：「能擇能守處，講者率多膚淺，非所以語顏子也。此作能槩括其梗槩，而探索其淵微，理到而文自工，過時輩遠矣。」

translation_en:
…there is naturally a sincerity that wins trust without admonition. When the work of reverence and reciprocity is fully accomplished and the result of freedom from resentment is attained, benevolence lies in nothing beyond this. If that result has not yet been attained, the work has not yet reached completion. Yong, should you not know how to examine yourself in this respect and thereby exert yourself further? Yet benevolence is one: why do the principles of reverence and reciprocity seem unlike the teaching of overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety? Heaven, in bringing things into being, nurtures them according to their capacities. The sage likewise teaches people according to the individual, seeking only that they achieve something. Nevertheless, reverence alone can extend throughout the higher and lower levels, and reciprocity, too, must not be regarded lightly. If one can truly devote oneself to these and gain understanding, there will eventually be no self left to overcome [?].

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
陳言而晦塞題意者相去何如蓋玩理而有心得者
考試官教諭林批詞藻沛然了無纖麗習氣
可爲鳴盛之作矣讀之一倡三歎
考試官教授陳批根理之言自是典雅且氣充
才贍而筆端有力非名士不及此
聖人稱大賢之於道擇之精而守之固也蓋擇
善固難而守善尤難大賢能擇能守此所以見
稱於聖人也歟昔子思因道之所以不明故引
夫子稱美顏子之言有曰天下有一定之理而
===
昧焉者不能擇人心有一定之操而惰焉者不
能守吾見回之爲人也以明健之資加好學之
篤知道之散於事者不能無過與不及也則必
隨事觀理辨之別之以求其所謂中庸者何在
理之寓於物者不能無過中失正也則必即物
窮理審之擇之以求其所謂中庸者何居精權
度於眾論之間務求至當不易之理有以要其
歸持藻鑑於兩端之際務求大中至正之道有
以見其的若然則其擇之也精矣及於辨別之
punctuated:
陳言而晦塞題意者，相去何如？蓋玩理而有心得者。
考試官教諭林批：詞藻沛然，了無纖麗習氣，可爲鳴盛之作矣。讀之一倡三歎。
考試官教授陳批：根理之言，自是典雅，且氣充才贍，而筆端有力，非名士不及此。
聖人稱大賢之於道，擇之精而守之固也。蓋擇善固難，而守善尤難。大賢能擇能守，此所以見稱於聖人也歟！昔子思因道之所以不明，故引夫子稱美顏子之言，有曰：「天下有一定之理，而昧焉者不能擇；人心有一定之操，而惰焉者不能守。吾見回之爲人也，以明健之資，加好學之篤，知道之散於事者，不能無過與不及也，則必隨事觀理，辨之別之，以求其所謂中庸者何在；理之寓於物者，不能無過中失正也，則必即物窮理，審之擇之，以求其所謂中庸者何居。精權度於眾論之間，務求至當不易之理，有以要其歸；持藻鑑於兩端之際，務求大中至正之道，有以見其的。若然，則其擇之也精矣。及於辨別之
translation_en:
…those who gather up stale expressions and obscure the meaning of the topic—how far apart are they from this writer? Surely this is someone who has pondered principle and attained his own understanding.
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: His literary expression flows abundantly, entirely free of the habitual taste for delicate ornament. This may serve as a work celebrating a flourishing age. Reading it is like hearing one voice lead and three respond in admiration.
Examiner Chen, Professor, comments: Words rooted in principle are naturally dignified and elegant. Moreover, his vital force is full, his talent abundant, and his brush powerful. None but a distinguished scholar could attain this.
The Sage praised the great worthy for choosing the Way with precision and holding to it firmly. For choosing what is good is certainly difficult, but holding to what is good is more difficult still. The great worthy could both choose and hold fast: was this not why he received the Sage’s praise? Formerly, Zisi, considering why the Way was not clearly understood, cited the Master’s words praising Master Yan, saying: “There is a fixed principle in the world, but those whose understanding is clouded cannot choose it; there is a fixed moral resolve in the human heart, but those who are indolent cannot maintain it. I observe that Hui, endowed with discernment and strength, and moreover deeply devoted to learning, knows that in the Way’s manifestation in affairs there inevitably occur excesses and deficiencies. He therefore invariably observes principle in each affair, distinguishing and discriminating, to discover where what is called the constant mean lies. In the embodiment of principle in things, there inevitably occur departures beyond the mean and losses of correctness. He therefore invariably investigates principle by approaching things, examining and selecting, to discover where what is called the constant mean resides. He refines his standards of judgment amid the many contending views, striving to find the supremely fitting and unchanging principle by which to grasp their ultimate purport. He exercises discerning judgment between the two extremes, striving to find the Way of perfect balance and utmost correctness by which to perceive the true target. In this way, his choosing is indeed precise. And when, in distinguishing and discriminating…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
餘得一中庸之道必拳拳而着之於心胷之間
務使理與心融而人欲不得以雜之審擇之際
得一中正之理必拳拳而着之於靈府之內務
使心與理契而私欲不得以間之會萬理於一
原曷嘗暫合遽離而復陷於過與不及之差乎
貫始終於一致何嘗暫得遽失而復淪於過中
失正之謬乎若然則其守之也固矣吁回之能
擇能守如此則非知者過之而不肖者之不及
也子思引之以見道之所由明也歟抑道在天
===
下欲明而行之惟存乎人〔共〕故必智如大舜而道
所以明仁如顏子而道所以行不然而欲道之明
之行難矣子思作中庸深為此懼故引大舜顏
淵之事以示人蓋欲人以智仁為入道之門不
致斯道終於不明不行也子思之功不亦大
乎
仁人心也義人路也
施信
同考試官訓導張批題本難體貼作者多不能
punctuated:
餘，得一中庸之道，必拳拳而着之於心胷之間，務使理與心融，而人欲不得以雜之。審擇之際，得一中正之理，必拳拳而着之於靈府之內，務使心與理契，而私欲不得以間之。會萬理於一原，曷嘗暫合遽離，而復陷於過與不及之差乎？貫始終於一致，何嘗暫得遽失，而復淪於過中失正之謬乎？若然，則其守之也固矣。吁！回之能擇能守如此，則非知者過之而不肖者之不及也。子思引之，以見道之所由明也歟？抑道在天下，欲明而行之，惟存乎人〔共〕。故必智如大舜，而道所以明；仁如顏子，而道所以行。不然而欲道之明之行，難矣！子思作《中庸》，深為此懼，故引大舜、顏淵之事以示人，蓋欲人以智仁為入道之門，不致斯道終於不明不行也。子思之功，不亦大乎？

仁，人心也；義，人路也。
施信
同考試官訓導張批：題本難體貼，作者多不能
translation_en:
…after making distinctions, whenever he apprehended a principle of the Mean, he would earnestly hold it within his heart, striving to make principle and mind blend together so that human desires could not adulterate it. In examining and choosing, whenever he apprehended a principle of centrality and correctness, he would earnestly hold it within the inner seat of his mind, striving to make mind accord with principle so that selfish desires could not come between them. Uniting the myriad principles in a single source, how could he ever briefly join with it and abruptly depart, falling once more into the errors of excess and deficiency? Maintaining a single consistency from beginning to end, how could he ever briefly attain it and abruptly lose it, sinking once more into the error of overshooting the mean and losing correctness? Thus his hold upon it was firm indeed. Ah! Hui's ability to choose and hold fast was such that he was neither among the knowing who go beyond it nor among the unworthy who fall short. Did Zisi cite him to show how the Way becomes clear? Yet, as the Way exists throughout the world, its clarification and practice depend upon people alone.〔“Together” [?].〕 Thus only with wisdom like that of the great Shun can the Way become clear, and only with benevolence like that of Master Yan can the Way be put into practice. Otherwise, to wish for the Way to become clear and be practiced is difficult indeed! In composing the Doctrine of the Mean, Zisi deeply feared this outcome. He therefore cited the deeds of the great Shun and Yan Yuan to instruct people, wishing them to take wisdom and benevolence as the gateway into the Way, so that it would not remain forever obscure and unpracticed. Was not Zisi's contribution great indeed?

“Benevolence is the human heart; righteousness is the human path.”
Shi Xin

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
據理摹寫每下筆不覺便有差句此篇詞理俱精到講人
心處更融會親切殆非草草於心學者
考試官教諭林批朱傳鮮仁義與他處自别
此作辯認既真故語自不苟當不以富麗求之也
考試官教授陳批破渾厚講尤不疎說理文
字正可作式於此故錄之
大賢揭所性之大而著其切於人焉蓋性莫大
於仁義而仁義實切於人身也自非大賢各舉
而名之何以知其然哉昔孟子之意語夫語理
===
於茫昧則人難知孰若名之於切近而人易曉
哉是故立人之道有所謂仁也人皆知其曰仁
而已孰知仁之所以為仁其切於已乎蓋仁也
者即人之心也四端之善兼統於方寸之間萬
善之元囊括於一腔之内寂然不動一生意之
充周所謂虛靈不昧者此也感而遂通一善念
之蘊藉所謂神妙不測者此也夫有是心即有
是仁外心以言仁則心為血肉之軀耳豈人心
之外别有所謂仁哉立人之道有所謂義也人
punctuated:
據理摹寫，每下筆不覺便有差句。此篇詞理俱精到，講人心處更融會親切，殆非草草於心學者。
考試官教諭林批：朱傳鮮仁義，與他處自别。此作辯認既真，故語自不苟，當不以富麗求之也。
考試官教授陳批：破渾厚，講尤不疎。說理文字，正可作式於此，故錄之。
大賢揭所性之大，而著其切於人焉。蓋性莫大於仁義，而仁義實切於人身也。自非大賢各舉而名之，何以知其然哉？昔孟子之意，語夫語理於茫昧，則人難知，孰若名之於切近，而人易曉哉？是故立人之道，有所謂仁也。人皆知其曰仁而已，孰知仁之所以為仁，其切於已乎？蓋仁也者，即人之心也。四端之善，兼統於方寸之間；萬善之元，囊括於一腔之内。寂然不動，一生意之充周，所謂虛靈不昧者此也；感而遂通，一善念之蘊藉，所謂神妙不測者此也。夫有是心，即有是仁。外心以言仁，則心為血肉之軀耳，豈人心之外别有所謂仁哉？立人之道，有所謂義也。人
translation_en:
…in depicting things in accordance with principle, whenever they put brush to paper they unwittingly produce erroneous phrases. This essay is accomplished in both expression and reasoning. Its discussion of the human heart is especially coherent and intimately pertinent; its author can hardly have been careless in studying the heart.
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: Zhu Xi’s commentary explains [?] benevolence and righteousness here differently from elsewhere. This essay distinguishes and identifies their meanings correctly, and thus its language is never careless. It should not be judged by richness and elegance of expression.
Examiner Chen, Professor, comments: The opening is substantial and rounded, and the exposition is particularly thorough. As writing that elucidates principle, this can rightly serve as a model; hence its inclusion.
The great worthy brought to light the greatest elements of our endowed nature and made clear their intimate relevance to human beings. For nothing in our nature is greater than benevolence and righteousness, and these are indeed intimately relevant to our own persons. Had the great worthy not singled out and named each, how could we have known this? Mencius’s intention in former times was to say [?]: if principle is discussed in obscure terms, people find it difficult to understand. How could this compare with naming it through what is close at hand, so that people can readily comprehend it?
Thus, in the Way by which human beings are established, there is what is called benevolence. People all know merely that it is called benevolence; who understands what makes benevolence benevolence, and how intimately it concerns oneself? Benevolence is precisely the human heart. The goodness of the four beginnings is comprehensively embraced within that tiny space; the source of all goodness is contained within this single breast. Still and unmoving, it is filled throughout with the impulse of life: this is what is meant by being empty, numinous, and unobscured. Responding to stimuli and thereupon penetrating all things, it holds within itself a good thought: this is what is meant by being wondrous and unfathomable. Wherever this heart exists, this benevolence exists. If one speaks of benevolence apart from the heart, then the heart becomes merely a bodily thing of flesh and blood. Could there be something separately called benevolence outside the human heart?
In the Way by which human beings are established, there is what is called righteousness. People…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
皆知其曰義而已孰知義之所以為義其切於
身乎蓋義也者即人之路也天理當行實為踐
履之地人事質幹允為蹈迪之途無偏無黨一
蕩蕩之康莊所謂周道如砥者是也無反無側
一平平之大道所謂其直如矢者是也夫有是
義即有是路外路以言義則路為邪曲之徑耳
豈人路之外別有所謂義哉仁而謂之人心則
可以見其為此身酬酢萬變之主而不可須臾
失矣義而謂之人路則可以見其為出入往來
===
必由之道而不可須臾舍矣仁義之切於人如
此人可不知所以求之哉雖然仁義根於人心
之固有何假聖賢之立名邪天下不知易故孔
子以生生名易天下不知中故子思以喜怒哀
樂名中天下溺於功利而不知有仁義故孟子
以人心人路名仁義蓋非聖賢意也覺天下之
不知者也聖賢立言垂訓每如此而人猶有放
其心而不求舍其路而不由者亦獨何心哉
易
punctuated:
皆知其曰義而已，孰知義之所以為義，其切於身乎？蓋義也者，即人之路也。天理當行，實為踐履之地；人事質幹，允為蹈迪之途。無偏無黨，一蕩蕩之康莊，所謂周道如砥者是也；無反無側，一平平之大道，所謂其直如矢者是也。夫有是義，即有是路；外路以言義，則路為邪曲之徑耳，豈人路之外別有所謂義哉？仁而謂之人心，則可以見其為此身酬酢萬變之主，而不可須臾失矣；義而謂之人路，則可以見其為出入往來必由之道，而不可須臾舍矣。仁義之切於人如此，人可不知所以求之哉？雖然，仁義根於人心之固有，何假聖賢之立名邪？天下不知易，故孔子以生生名易；天下不知中，故子思以喜怒哀樂名中；天下溺於功利而不知有仁義，故孟子以人心人路名仁義。蓋非聖賢意也，覺天下之不知者也。聖賢立言垂訓每如此，而人猶有放其心而不求、舍其路而不由者，亦獨何心哉？

易
translation_en:
…all know only that it is called righteousness. Who understands what makes righteousness righteousness, and how closely it concerns oneself? Righteousness is the path of human beings. Where heavenly principle ought to be put into practice is indeed the ground upon which one must tread; the essential substance of human affairs is truly the course one must follow. Without partiality or faction, it is a broad and open thoroughfare: this is what is meant by “the road of Zhou is like a whetstone.” Without deviation or inclination to either side, it is a level highway: this is what is meant by “straight as an arrow.” Where there is this righteousness, there is this path. To speak of righteousness apart from the path would leave the path merely a crooked and perverse track. Could there be a separate thing called righteousness outside the human path?

Calling benevolence the human heart shows that it is the master by which one responds to the myriad changes of affairs, and that it must not be lost even for an instant. Calling righteousness the human path shows that it is the way one must follow in all one’s comings and goings, and that it must not be abandoned even for an instant. Since benevolence and righteousness concern human beings so intimately, can people fail to know how to seek them?

Yet benevolence and righteousness are rooted in what the human heart inherently possesses. What need is there for sages and worthies to give them names? Because the world did not understand change, Kongzi defined change through unceasing generation. Because the world did not understand equilibrium, Zisi defined equilibrium through joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure. Because the world was submerged in achievement and profit and did not know that benevolence and righteousness existed, Mengzi defined benevolence and righteousness as the human heart and the human path. These were not notions invented by the sages and worthies; they served to awaken those in the world who did not understand. Such is always the way in which sages and worthies establish their teachings and transmit their instruction. Yet there are still people who let their hearts stray without seeking them and abandon their path without following it. What sort of heart can they possibly have?

Book of Changes (Yijing)

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
六二鴻漸于磐飲食衎衎吉
陸鈳
同考試官教諭唐批
文詞中發出人臣事君
之義他日不苟於祿位可以占矣
同考試官教諭蔡批
豐贍中典雅自存非
才富而理到者不能得士如此可以冠本房矣
同考試官教諭郁批
本爻生意出處之義
畢見佳作也
考試官教諭林批
命意造詞皆在經傳
===
中出沒惟深於易者能之
考試官教授陳批
理明詞贍
漸之六二有進得其所之象有進獲乎善之占
蓋進以有德有應為貴也六二兼之則其進之
安而善之獲也有以哉周公繫爻之意以為君
子之仕也不以爵祿之榮為念而以出處之正
為難漸之六二柔順中正而得漸進之道上應
九五而有可進之機則是為人臣者外比於賢
宅俊於我乎是職有高而不危之休也上麗大
punctuated:
六二，鴻漸于磐，飲食衎衎，吉。
陸鈳。
同考試官教諭唐批：文詞中發出人臣事君之義，他日不苟於祿位，可以占矣。

translation_en:
“Six in the second place: The wild goose gradually advances to the rock. It eats and drinks in contentment. Auspicious.”
Lu Ke 陸鈳.
Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor, comments: “The language brings out the principles governing a minister’s service to his ruler. From this one may predict that in future he will not be careless about accepting salary and office.”
Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor, comments: “Amid its richness and amplitude, classical elegance remains intact. Only someone of abundant talent and thorough understanding of principle could achieve this. Having obtained a candidate like this, we may rank him first in this examining section.”
Associate Examiner Yu, Instructor, comments: “The vital meaning of this line and the principles governing service and withdrawal are fully revealed. An excellent composition.”
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: “Both the conception of its meaning and the crafting of its language move throughout the classic and its commentaries. Only someone deeply versed in the Book of Changes could accomplish this.”
Examiner Chen, Professor, comments: “Clear reasoning and ample language.”
The second six of Gradual Progress presents an image of advancing to one’s proper place and a prognostication of attaining good through advancement. For what matters in advancement is possessing virtue and having a corresponding line. The second six possesses both: surely there is a basis for its secure advancement and attainment of good! The intention behind the Duke of Zhou’s appended statement on this line is that, when a gentleman takes office, he does not concern himself with the glory of rank and salary, but regards acting rightly in serving or withdrawing as the difficult task. The second six of Gradual Progress is yielding and compliant, central and correct, and thus accords with the way of gradual advancement. Above, it corresponds to the nine in the fifth place, and thus has an opportunity to advance. Accordingly, one serving as a minister associates outwardly with worthy men; this is an office in which I am appointed as a man of talent [?], bringing the blessing of standing high without peril. Above, he attaches himself to the great …

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
明公孤於我乎是任無處非其據之嫌也於是
享鼎之大烹而優游於見食於人之時俯仰何
愧怍乎受夬之施祿而委蛇於退食自公之際
情意何順乎適殆猶鴻焉將翱將翔漸于磐石
而棲止之自安也以飲以啄遠於水涯而和樂
之自若也其象如此其占維何蓋德薄而位尊
者必來負乘之誚功卑而祿崇者難免素餐之
譏今既有德而有應吾知其譽達於顯比之君
而朱紱方來有以荷天休之滋至道行於孚嘉
===
之日而大車以載足以勝重任而不疑平居之
抱負發而為俊偉之事功天位與共三公不為
尊也言孰加焉疇昔之涵養措而為光大之勳
業天祿與食萬鍾不為泰也吉孰尚焉夫以君
子之不苟於進而進得所安如此其君臣相遇
之際殆非偶然者周公以是而著六二爻義其
示占者之意深矣抑考此爻之義古之人有行
之者伊呂是也觀其保衡商家弼成周室厥功
偉矣然使成湯無三聘之勤而文王無後車之
punctuated: 明，公孤於我乎是任，無處非其據之嫌也。於是享鼎之大烹，而優游於見食於人之時，俯仰何愧怍乎？受夬之施祿，而委蛇於退食自公之際，情意何順乎適？殆猶鴻焉，將翱將翔，漸于磐石，而棲止之自安也；以飲以啄，遠於水涯，而和樂之自若也。其象如此，其占維何？蓋德薄而位尊者，必來負乘之誚；功卑而祿崇者，難免素餐之譏。今既有德而有應，吾知其譽達於顯比之君，而朱紱方來，有以荷天休之滋至；道行於孚嘉之日，而大車以載，足以勝重任而不疑。平居之抱負，發而為俊偉之事功，天位與共，三公不為尊也，言孰加焉？疇昔之涵養，措而為光大之勳業，天祿與食，萬鍾不為泰也，吉孰尚焉？夫以君子之不苟於進，而進得所安如此，其君臣相遇之際，殆非偶然者。周公以是而著六二爻義，其示占者之意深矣！抑考此爻之義，古之人有行之者，伊呂是也。觀其保衡商家，弼成周室，厥功偉矣。然使成湯無三聘之勤，而文王無後車之
translation_en:
…illumination; entrusted with the duties of a duke or junior guardian, I incur no suspicion of occupying a position that is not rightfully mine. Thus, enjoying the great feast of the Cauldron hexagram, he rests at ease while receiving sustenance from others: whether looking down or up, what cause has he for shame? Receiving the distribution of emoluments represented by the Resolution hexagram, he moves at leisure as he withdraws from public service to take his meal: how harmonious and content his feelings are [?]. He is much like a wild goose, spreading its wings and taking flight, gradually advancing to a great rock and settling there securely; drinking and pecking, far from the water’s edge, it remains naturally peaceful and happy. Such is the image; what, then, is its prognostication?

Those whose virtue is meager but whose rank is high inevitably invite the reproach of “carrying a burden while riding in a carriage”; those whose achievements are slight but whose emoluments are generous can scarcely escape criticism for eating without earning their keep. Now, possessing both virtue and a corresponding response above, he will, I know, win recognition from a ruler who openly seeks worthy associates. The vermilion knee-covering of office will soon come, enabling him to receive Heaven’s blessings in increasing abundance. His Way will prevail when sincerity meets with approval; like a great wagon bearing its load, he will be fully capable of carrying weighty responsibilities, without doubt. The aspirations he has cherished in ordinary life will emerge as outstanding achievements in office. Sharing in Heaven-conferred rank, he will not find even the position of one of the Three Dukes too exalted. What praise could surpass this? The self-cultivation of former days will be put to work in illustrious accomplishments. Sharing in Heaven-conferred emoluments, he will not find even ten thousand measures of grain excessive. What good fortune could exceed this?

Since the gentleman does not seek advancement heedlessly, yet advances to a position in which he finds such security, his encounter with his ruler can hardly be accidental. On this basis, the Duke of Zhou set forth the meaning of the six in the second place. Profound indeed was his intention in instructing those who consult the oracle! Moreover, examining the meaning of this line, we find men of antiquity who put it into practice: Yi Yin and Lü Shang. Consider how one served as chief counselor to the house of Shang and the other assisted in establishing the house of Zhou: their achievements were great indeed. Yet had Cheng Tang not diligently extended three invitations, and had King Wen not, in the carriage following his own, …

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
載則二公之志亦終於莘野渭濱而已是知行
道者君子之本心而所以得行其道者則顧所
遇何如耳後世之士汲汲以仕進爲心而昧於
出處之宜蓋亦不占而已矣
乾之策二百一十有六坤之策百四十有
四凡三百有六十當朞之日二篇之策萬
有一千五百二十當萬物之數也
趙廷富
同考試官教諭唐批蓍策一題多病於詞說之
贅此篇明白簡當非衆作可及其精於理學者與
同考試官教諭蔡批蓍數最爲微妙子能探
而發之錄之以式來學
同考試官教諭郝批此題重在當朞之日與當
萬物之數士子類無的見挑剔明白僅見此篇噫若子
者可以語數學矣
考試官教諭林批數學最難而子能言之
可嘉
考試官教授陳批蓍數之妙此作盡之
punctuated:
載，則二公之志亦終於莘野、渭濱而已。是知行道者，君子之本心，而所以得行其道者，則顧所遇何如耳。後世之士汲汲以仕進爲心，而昧於出處之宜，蓋亦不占而已矣。

乾之策二百一十有六，坤之策百四十有四，凡三百有六十，當朞之日。二篇之策萬有一千五百二十，當萬物之數也。

趙廷富

同考試官教諭唐批：「蓍策一題，多病於詞說之贅。此篇明白簡當，非衆作可及，其精於理學者與！」

同考試官教諭蔡批：「蓍數最爲微妙，子能探而發之，錄之以式來學。」

同考試官教諭郝批：「此題重在當朞之日與當萬物之數，士子類無的見。挑剔明白，僅見此篇。噫！若子者，可以語數學矣。」

考試官教諭林批：「數學最難，而子能言之，可嘉。」

考試官教授陳批：「蓍數之妙，此作盡之。」
translation_en:
…to carry him, then the aspirations of those two worthies would likewise have ended in the fields of Shen and on the banks of the Wei. Thus we know that putting the Way into practice is the gentleman’s fundamental intention, but whether he can do so depends upon the circumstances he encounters. Scholars of later ages anxiously set their hearts upon advancement in office, yet fail to understand when it is proper to serve or withdraw. Surely they simply do not consult the divination!

“The stalk count for Qian is two hundred and sixteen; the stalk count for Kun is one hundred and forty-four. Together they total three hundred and sixty, corresponding to the days of a year. The stalk count for the two parts of the Book of Changes is eleven thousand five hundred and twenty, corresponding to the number of the myriad things.”

Zhao Tingfu 趙廷富

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: “On this topic of the divining-stalk counts, essays commonly suffer from excessive verbiage. This essay is clear, concise, and apt, beyond the reach of the other submissions. Surely its author is deeply versed in the learning of principle!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, Instructor: “The numbers of the divining stalks are exceedingly subtle. You have been able to investigate and elucidate them. This essay is recorded as a model for future students.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Hao, Instructor: “The emphasis of this topic lies in ‘corresponding to the days of a year’ and ‘corresponding to the number of the myriad things.’ Candidates generally lack a definite understanding of these points. Only this essay distinguishes and elucidates them clearly. Ah! With someone like you, one can discuss the learning of numbers.”

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: “The learning of numbers is most difficult, yet you can explain it. This deserves praise.”

Comment by Examiner Chen, Instructor: “This essay fully expounds the subtleties of the divining-stalk numbers.”

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
大傳論過揲之策有純卦之所準者有全經之
所準者蓋蓍数與造化相爲流通者也不自其
所準觀之何以見其妙哉大傳論数法至此則
以過揲之策生於河圖之四面者言之意謂数
雖具於蓍策妙實符乎造化何也蓋揲蓍三變
之末九六迭出之餘三竒而九四之則爲三十
有六也積而至於六畫之乾則爲三十有六者
凡六而得二百一十有六之策焉三偶而六四
之則爲二十有四也積而至於六畫之坤則爲
===
二十有四者凡六而得百四十有四之策焉以
乾策之二百一十有六合坤策之百四十有四
其爲数也凡三百有六十寧不有以當期之日
乎蓋一歲之日有氣盈有朔虚雖不能無多寡
之殊而三百六十乃其成数也二卦之策適與
之而相當初若有擬議焉者其妙也何如至若
乾爲陽物凡百九十二之陽爻散見於二篇者
皆乾也而其策莫非三十有六即是數而乗之
以諸陽則得夫六千九百一十二策焉坤爲陰
punctuated: 大傳論過揲之策，有純卦之所準者，有全經之所準者。蓋蓍数與造化相爲流通者也，不自其所準觀之，何以見其妙哉？大傳論数法至此，則以過揲之策生於河圖之四面者言之，意謂数雖具於蓍策，妙實符乎造化。何也？蓋揲蓍三變之末，九六迭出之餘，三竒而九，四之則爲三十有六也。積而至於六畫之乾，則爲三十有六者凡六，而得二百一十有六之策焉。三偶而六，四之則爲二十有四也。積而至於六畫之坤，則爲二十有四者凡六，而得百四十有四之策焉。以乾策之二百一十有六合坤策之百四十有四，其爲数也凡三百有六十，寧不有以當期之日乎？蓋一歲之日有氣盈，有朔虚，雖不能無多寡之殊，而三百六十乃其成数也。二卦之策適與之而相當，初若有擬議焉者，其妙也何如！至若乾爲陽物，凡百九十二之陽爻散見於二篇者皆乾也，而其策莫非三十有六。即是數而乗之以諸陽，則得夫六千九百一十二策焉。坤爲陰
translation_en:
The Great Commentary discusses the stalks remaining after counting off: some take the pure hexagrams as their standard, while others take the entire Classic as their standard. The numbers of the milfoil stalks and the processes of creation are interconnected. Unless we examine what these numbers correspond to, how can we perceive their subtlety? At this point in its discussion of numerical methods, the Great Commentary speaks of the remaining stalks as deriving from the four sides of the River Chart. Its meaning is that, although the numbers are embodied in the milfoil stalks, their subtle workings truly accord with creation. Why is this so?

At the end of the three operations of counting the milfoil stalks, after nine and six have emerged in turn, three odd results yield nine; multiplying this by four gives thirty-six. Accumulating these through the six lines of Qian gives six sets of thirty-six, yielding 216 stalks. Three even results yield six; multiplying this by four gives twenty-four. Accumulating these through the six lines of Kun gives six sets of twenty-four, yielding 144 stalks. Combining Qian’s 216 stalks with Kun’s 144 gives a total of 360. Does this not correspond to the days of a year? In the days of a year there is a surplus in the solar cycle and a deficit in the lunar cycle. Although differences in their totals are unavoidable, 360 is their integral count. The stalks of the two hexagrams correspond exactly to this, as though some deliberate calculation had been made. How subtle this is!

As for Qian, it represents yang entities. All 192 yang lines scattered throughout the two parts of the Classic belong to Qian, and each has thirty-six stalks. Taking this number and multiplying it by all the yang lines yields 6,912 stalks. Kun represents yin…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
物凡百九十二之陰爻分布於二篇者皆坤也
而其策莫非二十有四即是数而乗之以諸陰
則得夫四千六百八策焉以陽爻之六千九百
一十二策合陰爻之四千六百八策其為數也
凡萬有一千五百二十寧不有以當萬物之数
乎蓋天下之物有氣化有形化其数雖不止於
萬而萬有其多乃其常数也二篇之策適與之
而相當初若有比度焉者其妙也又何如是則
乾策坤策蓍數之一定也而於造化有所凖曰
===
数物数造化之有常也而於蓍策不能外筮法
之妙有如此夫抑斯論也蓋謂陽主乎進少陽
進而未極乎盈則不足以為化陰主乎退少陰
退而未極乎虛則不足以為變故卦之乾坤爻
之竒偶獨以二老計之至於以二少計之則其
數莫不有脗合焉者此亦夫子之意而諸儒之
說也
書
刑期于無刑
punctuated:
物，凡百九十二之陰爻分布於二篇者，皆坤也，而其策莫非二十有四。即是数而乗之以諸陰，則得夫四千六百八策焉。以陽爻之六千九百一十二策，合陰爻之四千六百八策，其為數也，凡萬有一千五百二十，寧不有以當萬物之数乎？蓋天下之物，有氣化，有形化，其数雖不止於萬，而萬有其多，乃其常数也。二篇之策適與之而相當，初若有比度焉者，其妙也又何如？是則乾策、坤策，蓍數之一定也，而於造化有所凖；曰数、物数，造化之有常也，而於蓍策不能外。筮法之妙有如此夫！抑斯論也，蓋謂陽主乎進，少陽進而未極乎盈，則不足以為化；陰主乎退，少陰退而未極乎虛，則不足以為變。故卦之乾坤，爻之竒偶，獨以二老計之。至於以二少計之，則其數莫不有脗合焉者。此亦夫子之意，而諸儒之說也。
書
刑期于無刑。
translation_en:
…entity. All 192 yin lines distributed throughout the two parts are Kun, and the stalk count for each is invariably twenty-four. Multiplying this number by all the yin lines yields 4,608 stalks. Adding the 6,912 stalks of the yang lines to the 4,608 stalks of the yin lines gives a total of 11,520. Does this not correspond to the number of the myriad things? The things under Heaven arise through transformations of vital energy or transformations of physical form. Although their number exceeds ten thousand, “ten thousand” expresses their multitude and is their conventional number. The stalk count of the two parts precisely corresponds to it, as though a comparison and reckoning had been made beforehand. How marvelous this too is! Thus the stalk counts of Qian and Kun are fixed numbers in yarrow-stalk divination, yet they have their counterparts in the processes of creation and transformation. The number of days [?] and the number of things are constants in creation and transformation, yet they cannot fall outside the reckoning of the yarrow stalks. Such is the marvelous character of the method of divination!
Now this argument means that yang chiefly advances: when young yang advances but has not reached complete fullness, it cannot bring about transformation. Yin chiefly retreats: when young yin retreats but has not reached complete emptiness, it cannot bring about change. Thus, for the hexagrams Qian and Kun and their odd and even lines, the calculation uses only old yang and old yin. As for calculations using young yang and young yin, their numbers likewise correspond in every case. This too is the Master's meaning and the explanation of the Confucian scholars.
Book of Documents
“The aim of punishments is to bring about the absence of punishment.”

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
俞振強
同考試官訓導張批題下難於遣詞而難於
上下文不相粘礙此作得之是宜録出
考試官教諭林批莊整可觀
考試官教授陳批此篇詞不繁而意自足
得作二典體
聖君稱士師始不免於刑之施心實期於刑之
措夫刑以不用為美也大臣於用刑之時而心
期於不用焉聖君稱之也宜哉昔帝舜不聴禹
===
之讓而稱臯陶之美以勸勉之若曰人但知汝
臯陶以刑為之職耳抑孰知其心存之美邪是
故臣工之多未必無違教者焉設或有之而刑
其可已乎汝為士師之官蓋嘗明以弼教而五
刑之是用矣民庶之衆未必無梗化者焉容或
有之而刑其可廢乎汝居掌刑之職蓋嘗明以
輔治而五刑之惟允矣墨也劓也推之而得其
情則舉以加之使知不善者有所懲剕宫也大
辟也審之而當其罪則因以施之使知為惡者
punctuated:
俞振強

同考試官訓導張批：題下難於遣詞，而難於上下文不相粘礙，此作得之，是宜録出。

考試官教諭林批：莊整可觀。

考試官教授陳批：此篇詞不繁而意自足，得作二典體。

聖君稱士師，始不免於刑之施，心實期於刑之措。夫刑以不用為美也，大臣於用刑之時，而心期於不用焉，聖君稱之也宜哉！昔帝舜不聴禹之讓，而稱臯陶之美以勸勉之，若曰：「人但知汝臯陶以刑為之職耳，抑孰知其心存之美邪？是故臣工之多，未必無違教者焉。設或有之，而刑其可已乎？汝為士師之官，蓋嘗明以弼教，而五刑之是用矣。民庶之衆，未必無梗化者焉。容或有之，而刑其可廢乎？汝居掌刑之職，蓋嘗明以輔治，而五刑之惟允矣。墨也，劓也，推之而得其情，則舉以加之，使知不善者有所懲；剕、宫也，大辟也，審之而當其罪，則因以施之，使知為惡者
translation_en:
Yu Zhenqiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Assistant Instructor: Beneath this topic, wording is difficult; it is also difficult to keep the preceding and following passages from overlapping and impeding one another. This composition succeeds in this respect and deserves to be selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: Dignified and well ordered, worthy of appreciation.

Comment by Examiner Chen, Professor: This piece is concise in wording yet complete in meaning. It achieves the style of the Two Canons.

The sage ruler praised his Director of Justice: although initially he could not avoid applying punishments, his heart truly aspired to lay them aside. For the finest use of punishment is to have no need to use it. When a great minister applies punishments yet in his heart hopes that they will cease to be needed, how fitting it is that the sage ruler should praise him!

Formerly, Emperor Shun did not accept Yu’s yielding of precedence, but praised Gao Yao’s excellence to encourage him, as though saying: “People know only that you, Gao Yao, have punishment as your official duty. Yet who understands the fine intentions you cherish in your heart? Among the many officials, there may well be some who transgress the teachings. If there are, can punishment be dispensed with? In your office as Director of Justice, you have indeed exercised discernment to support instruction, employing the five punishments. Among the multitude of common people, there may well be some who obstruct moral transformation. If there are, can punishment be abolished? Holding responsibility for punishments, you have indeed exercised discernment to assist government, ensuring that the five punishments are justly applied. Tattooing and cutting off the nose: when investigation establishes the facts of a case, you impose these, so that those who do wrong may know that misconduct brings chastisement. Amputation of the feet, castration, and death: when careful examination determines the punishment fitting the crime, you administer these, so that those who commit evil may know …

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
有所懼汝之不免於用刑者如是原汝之心豈
欲恃以為治邪將以致夫治隆之功使在朝廷
也禮義流行純乎道德之懿而刑法殆為虛器
矣將以收夫俗美之效使在閭閻也德化洋溢
藹乎淳朴之風而理官若為虛設矣一心之所
願直欲舉國皆遵其教而過焉有所不為則墨
劓之刑雖小不用焉一念之所存直欲舉世皆
從其化而罪焉決於不犯則剕宮大辟之典雖
重不施焉吁臯陶有無刑之期而今卒能副之
===
如此此伯禹之所以讓而帝舜所以稱之也歟
大抵聖人之治德為化民之本刑為輔治之法
然謂之輔則見其用於時者皆聖人之不得已
也有虞之刑司之以明慎之臯陶主之以欽恤
之帝舜尚不足以為恃必求至于不犯有司四
方風動而後已彼後世之鍛鍊以為能根連株
繫而不忌者獨何心哉
茲亦惟天若元德永不忘在王家
王鏞
punctuated:
有所懼。汝之不免於用刑者如是，原汝之心，豈欲恃以為治邪？將以致夫治隆之功，使在朝廷也，禮義流行，純乎道德之懿，而刑法殆為虛器矣；將以收夫俗美之效，使在閭閻也，德化洋溢，藹乎淳朴之風，而理官若為虛設矣。一心之所願，直欲舉國皆遵其教，而過焉有所不為，則墨劓之刑雖小，不用焉；一念之所存，直欲舉世皆從其化，而罪焉決於不犯，則剕宮大辟之典雖重，不施焉。吁！臯陶有無刑之期，而今卒能副之如此，此伯禹之所以讓，而帝舜所以稱之也歟！
大抵聖人之治，德為化民之本，刑為輔治之法。然謂之輔，則見其用於時者，皆聖人之不得已也。有虞之刑，司之以明慎之臯陶，主之以欽恤之帝舜，尚不足以為恃，必求至于不犯有司，四方風動而後已。彼後世之鍛鍊以為能，根連株繫而不忌者，獨何心哉？
茲亦惟天若元德，永不忘在王家。
王鏞
translation_en:
…have something to fear. Such are the circumstances in which you cannot avoid employing punishments. Yet, examining your heart, could you wish to rely upon them to govern? Your purpose is to achieve flourishing government, so that ritual propriety and righteousness prevail at court, imbued wholly with the excellence of the Way and virtue, and penal laws become little more than unused instruments. Your purpose is to bring about fine customs, so that virtue’s transforming influence overflows among the common people, an atmosphere of simplicity and sincerity abounds, and judicial officials seem to hold offices with nothing to do. Your heart’s sole desire is that the entire realm observe your teaching and refrain from wrongdoing; then even the lesser punishments of tattooing and cutting off the nose need not be used. Your every thought is that all under Heaven follow your transforming influence and firmly resolve not to commit crimes; then even the weightier penalties of amputating the feet, castration, and death need not be imposed. Ah! Gao Yao hoped for a time without punishments, and now at last he has fulfilled that hope in this way. Was this not why Bo Yu yielded precedence to him and Emperor Shun praised him?
In general, in the sages’ government, virtue is the foundation for transforming the people, and punishment is a means of assisting government. Yet calling it an assistance shows that whenever the sages employed it, they did so only because they had no alternative. The punishments of Youyu were administered by the discerning and cautious Gao Yao and overseen by the reverent and compassionate Emperor Shun. Even so, these were not sufficient to rely upon: they would not rest until the people no longer ran afoul of the responsible authorities and all four quarters responded as grass bends before the wind. What, then, was in the hearts of those in later ages who counted the fabrication of criminal cases as an accomplishment and had no scruples about implicating and binding together everyone connected with the accused, root and branch?
“This, too, is Heaven’s accordance with great virtue, which shall never be forgotten in the royal house.”
Wang Yong.

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導張批兹字只指稽德饋祀而
言元德亦不過此士子乃併前羞考說來於元德上卒
無歸着惟此篇體貼經傳作出且文氣老成規度嚴肅
宜錄之以式
考試官教諭林批簡實可觀
考試官教授陳批理明詞順可取可取
聖君教妹臣能有謹酒之實則膺天眷於無窮
矣夫天之休命得之固難而有永尤難也非妹
臣有謹酒之實天之所眷豈若是哉昔者武王
===
告康叔欲其教妹土之臣也其意謂夫汝庶士
有正庶伯君子母以脩德為無益謹酒為小德
也誠能反觀内省悉稽乎中正之德而有盛大
之實克羞饋祀自用夫宴樂之飲而無沉湎之
累如此有不足以得天者乎吾知禍福不常天
至難諶也鑒此元德自有以順之於冲漠之中
予奪靡定天未易得也眷此大德自有以若之
於亭毒之表天非有私於汝也而富貴以厚其
生者方興而未艾汝非有求於天也而福澤以
punctuated:
同考試官訓導張批：「兹字只指稽德饋祀而言，元德亦不過此。士子乃併前羞考說來，於元德上卒無歸着。惟此篇體貼經傳作出，且文氣老成，規度嚴肅，宜錄之以式。」
考試官教諭林批：「簡實可觀。」
考試官教授陳批：「理明詞順，可取可取。」
聖君教妹臣能有謹酒之實，則膺天眷於無窮矣。夫天之休命，得之固難，而有永尤難也。非妹臣有謹酒之實，天之所眷豈若是哉？昔者武王告康叔，欲其教妹土之臣也。其意謂夫汝庶士、有正、庶伯、君子，母以脩德為無益、謹酒為小德也。誠能反觀内省，悉稽乎中正之德，而有盛大之實，克羞饋祀，自用夫宴樂之飲，而無沉湎之累，如此，有不足以得天者乎？吾知禍福不常，天至難諶也；鑒此元德，自有以順之於冲漠之中。予奪靡定，天未易得也；眷此大德，自有以若之於亭毒之表。天非有私於汝也，而富貴以厚其生者方興而未艾；汝非有求於天也，而福澤以
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zhang, an Assistant Instructor, comments: “The word ‘this’ refers only to examining one’s virtue and presenting sacrificial offerings; ‘great virtue’ likewise means no more than this. Candidates bring in the preceding phrase about presenting offerings to deceased fathers, but ultimately fail to give ‘great virtue’ a definite meaning. This essay alone is composed in close accord with the classic and its commentary. Its prose is mature, its structure disciplined and dignified. It should be recorded as a model.”
Examiner Lin, an Instructor, comments: “Concise and substantial; worthy of attention.”
Examiner Chen, a Professor, comments: “Clear in reasoning and fluent in expression. Worth accepting, worth accepting!”
When the sage ruler teaches the ministers of Mei [?] to exercise genuine restraint in drinking, they will receive Heaven’s favor without end. Heaven’s gracious mandate is certainly difficult to obtain, but perpetuating it is harder still. Unless the ministers of Mei [?] genuinely exercised restraint in drinking, how could Heaven favor them in this way? Formerly, King Wu addressed Kang Shu, intending that he instruct the ministers in the territory of Mei [?]. His meaning was this: You officers, heads of offices, chiefs, and gentlemen must not regard cultivating virtue as useless or restraint in drinking as a minor virtue. If you can truly examine yourselves inwardly, take upright and balanced virtue as your standard in all things, and substantially embody its greatness; if you can present sacrificial offerings and yourselves enjoy wine at feasts without the burden of drunken excess—would anything then be lacking in your capacity to win Heaven’s favor? I know that calamity and blessing are inconstant, and that Heaven is exceedingly difficult to trust. Yet, discerning this great virtue, Heaven will naturally respond favorably within its silent, formless workings. Its granting and withholding are unsettled, and Heaven’s favor is not easily obtained. Yet, regarding this great virtue, Heaven will naturally accord with it beyond the manifest workings of its nurturing power. Heaven shows you no partiality, yet the wealth and honor that enrich your lives are just beginning to flourish and have not ceased. You ask nothing of Heaven, yet blessings and bounty, by which …

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
庇其身者滋至而無已曰名曰位昔固見錄於
王家矣今則居之安而綿綿不絕不但居之一
時也將歷悠久而常保矣豈復有瑕殄者乎曰
職曰禄昔嘗見錫於王家矣今則守之固而源
源不竭非但守之一時也將至悠遠而常享矣
寧復有棄絕者乎吁武王欲其臣之謹酒而舉
天若元德為勸如此其亦誘掖之至者歟嗟夫
妹土臣民蕞爾之微耳况以康叔往為之君宜
其無難化者武王乃致告之如此者何哉蓋商
===
受酗酒天下化之而妹土為其故都染惡尤深
武王誅君弔民一新其政孰有急於是邪禹於
子孫嘗有甘酒之訓成湯風愆之戒亦以酣歌
寓乎其間古昔聖人未嘗不拳拳于是也噫彼
昏不知隄糟池酒者何哉
詩
考卜維王宅是鎬京維龜正之武王成之
王容
同考試官教諭何 批 稽疑決疑處作者多挑剔
punctuated:
庇其身者滋至而無已。曰名曰位，昔固見錄於王家矣，今則居之安而綿綿不絕，不但居之一時也，將歷悠久而常保矣，豈復有瑕殄者乎？曰職曰禄，昔嘗見錫於王家矣，今則守之固而源源不竭，非但守之一時也，將至悠遠而常享矣，寧復有棄絕者乎？吁！武王欲其臣之謹酒，而舉天若元德為勸，如此，其亦誘掖之至者歟！嗟夫！妹土臣民，蕞爾之微耳，况以康叔往為之君，宜其無難化者。武王乃致告之如此者何哉？蓋商受酗酒，天下化之，而妹土為其故都，染惡尤深。武王誅君弔民，一新其政，孰有急於是邪？禹於子孫嘗有甘酒之訓，成湯風愆之戒，亦以酣歌寓乎其間。古昔聖人未嘗不拳拳于是也。噫！彼昏不知隄，糟池酒者何哉？

詩

考卜維王，宅是鎬京。維龜正之，武王成之。

王容

同考試官教諭何批：稽疑決疑處，作者多挑剔
translation_en:
…the blessings that shelter you will arrive in ever greater abundance, without end. As for reputation and rank, you formerly received recognition from the royal house; now you will hold them securely, in unbroken succession. You will possess them not merely for a time, but preserve them through long ages. How could there again be harm or extinction? As for office and emoluments, you formerly received them from the royal house; now you will keep them firmly, flowing continuously without exhaustion. You will retain them not merely for a time, but enjoy them into the distant future. How could there again be rejection or severance? Ah! King Wu wished his ministers to exercise restraint in drinking, and encouraged them by invoking Heaven’s favor toward great virtue. Was this not the utmost in guidance and assistance?

Alas! The ministers and people of Mei were but a tiny community. Moreover, Kang Shu was going there to become their ruler, so surely they should not have been difficult to transform. Why, then, did King Wu admonish them in this manner? Because Shou of Shang drank to excess, and all under Heaven followed his example. Mei, being his former capital, was especially deeply tainted by this evil. King Wu punished its ruler, comforted its people, and entirely renewed its government. What could have been more urgent than this? Yu once admonished his descendants against delighting in wine. Cheng Tang’s warning against the fault of dissolute conduct likewise included drunken singing. The sages of antiquity never failed to give this matter their earnest attention. Alas! What of those benighted men who knew no restraint, with their dregs and pools of wine [?]?

The Book of Odes

“Having examined the divination, the king established his dwelling here at Haojing. The tortoise determined it; King Wu brought it to completion.”

Wang Rong

Comment by Associate Examiner He, Instructor: In dealing with the consultation of divination and the resolution of doubts, writers often pick apart…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不明此作認題精確而詞又足以發之令人拭目
同考試官教諭戴批剖析詳明而詞意警拔駸
駸然追逼古作蓋不梏於專經者
同考試官教諭吳批作此篇者形容都遷氣象
綺語動盈卷帙顧於遷都不苟處不相發此作因題命
意根理遣詞使武王當年心事宛然在目竒士也
考試官教諭林批氣昌理到掃去陳言時
作中不多得
考試官教授陳批詞豊贍而意圓活宜錄
===
以式承學
稽諸神以定都决諸神以建都詩人美聖君然
也夫遷都國之大事也聖君必稽於神而後决
焉其慎重之意何如哉此詩美武王遷鎬而作
也蓋謂我武王當四方攸同之日遂有遷都于
鎬之舉以為開國承家非細故也烏可苟哉與
其謀於人也不若謀之於神乃考之於卜于以
决吉凶於猶豫之間與其斷於己也不若斷之
於神乃稽之於占于以質休咎於疑似之頃遷此
punctuated:
不明。此作認題精確，而詞又足以發之，令人拭目。
同考試官教諭戴批：剖析詳明，而詞意警拔，駸駸然追逼古作，蓋不梏於專經者。
同考試官教諭吳批：作此篇者，形容都遷氣象，綺語動盈卷帙，顧於遷都不苟處不相發。此作因題命意，根理遣詞，使武王當年心事宛然在目，竒士也。
考試官教諭林批：氣昌理到，掃去陳言，時作中不多得。
考試官教授陳批：詞豊贍而意圓活，宜錄以式承學。
稽諸神以定都，决諸神以建都，詩人美聖君然也。夫遷都，國之大事也，聖君必稽於神而後决焉，其慎重之意何如哉！此詩美武王遷鎬而作也。蓋謂我武王當四方攸同之日，遂有遷都于鎬之舉，以為開國承家，非細故也，烏可苟哉！與其謀於人也，不若謀之於神，乃考之於卜，于以决吉凶於猶豫之間；與其斷於己也，不若斷之於神，乃稽之於占，于以質休咎於疑似之頃。遷此
translation_en:
…do not understand clearly. This essay grasps the topic precisely, and its language fully brings out its meaning: it makes one look afresh.
Associate Examiner Dai, Instructor, comments: Its analysis is detailed and clear, and its language and ideas are striking and distinguished. It presses swiftly toward the achievements of ancient writings. Here is someone not constrained by specialization in a single Classic.
Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor, comments: Those who compose essays on this passage describe the spectacle of the capital’s relocation, readily filling whole volumes with ornate language, yet fail to bring out the care with which the relocation was undertaken. This essay develops its argument from the topic and grounds its wording in principle, making King Wu’s thoughts at that time appear vividly before our eyes. An exceptional talent!
Examiner Lin, Instructor, comments: Its spirit is vigorous and its reasoning thorough; it sweeps away stale expressions. Such writing is seldom found among contemporary essays.
Examiner Chen, Professor, comments: Its language is rich and ample, and its ideas rounded and supple. It should be recorded as a model for students.
He consulted the spirits to determine the site of the capital and sought their decision in establishing it: this is what the poet praises in the sage ruler. Relocating the capital is a great affair of state. The sage ruler must consult the spirits before deciding. How profound his care and caution! This poem was composed to praise King Wu’s relocation to Hao. It says, in effect, that when the lands in all four directions had united under our King Wu, he undertook to move the capital to Hao. He considered that founding a state and securing its ruling house were no trifling matters: how could he act carelessly? Rather than consult people, it was better to consult the spirits. He therefore examined the matter through turtle-shell divination, resolving whether the outcome would be auspicious or inauspicious while uncertainty remained. Rather than decide by himself, it was better to seek a decision from the spirits. He therefore investigated the prognostications, ascertaining good or ill fortune while doubt remained. In relocating to this…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
鎬京必欲得形勝而據之建宗社營宫室居重
馭輕而爲萬國都會之區也居此鎬京必欲得
險阻而依之築城邑立朝市宅中圖大而垂萬
世無疆之休也于斯時也灼彼元龜適有以協
人謀考成象於墨食之初有吉而無凶也先矣
王者之都向之猶豫以决燃彼楚焞適有以符
已見驗成卦於鑽刺之後有休而無咎也信矣
邦畿之地昔之疑似以定於是斷自宸衷據此
天下之形勝宗社以建宫室以營制度煥乎其
===
聿新也所謂萬邦之方者在是出自睿筭依此
天下之險阻城邑以築朝市以立規模秩乎其
鼎建也所謂下民之王者在是吁武王遷鎬必
决之神謀而不敢焉苟如此君道之盡不於此
而可見乎詩人所以美之也宜矣大抵遷都所
以爲民而出於爲民之外者皆私也亦所以爲
後世謀而爲後亦爲民也武王之遷鎬以豐邑
難容而遷是故爲民而遷耳遷之而謀無不悉
亦爲民而謀焉耳視彼後世若長安之都惟圖
punctuated: 鎬京，必欲得形勝而據之，建宗社，營宫室，居重馭輕，而爲萬國都會之區也。居此鎬京，必欲得險阻而依之，築城邑，立朝市，宅中圖大，而垂萬世無疆之休也。于斯時也，灼彼元龜，適有以協人謀；考成象於墨食之初，有吉而無凶也，先矣，王者之都，向之猶豫以决。燃彼楚焞，適有以符已見；驗成卦於鑽刺之後，有休而無咎也，信矣，邦畿之地，昔之疑似以定。於是斷自宸衷，據此天下之形勝，宗社以建，宫室以營，制度煥乎其聿新也，所謂萬邦之方者在是。出自睿筭，依此天下之險阻，城邑以築，朝市以立，規模秩乎其鼎建也，所謂下民之王者在是。吁！武王遷鎬，必决之神謀，而不敢焉苟如此，君道之盡，不於此而可見乎？詩人所以美之也，宜矣。大抵遷都，所以爲民，而出於爲民之外者，皆私也。亦所以爲後世謀，而爲後亦爲民也。武王之遷鎬，以豐邑難容而遷，是故爲民而遷耳。遷之而謀無不悉，亦爲民而謀焉耳。視彼後世，若長安之都，惟圖
translation_en:
…to Haojing, he was determined to secure and occupy a strategically advantageous site, establish the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain, and construct palaces, making it a commanding center from which to govern the outlying regions and a capital where the myriad states would converge. In settling at Haojing, he was determined to secure and rely upon natural defenses, build city walls, and establish the court and markets, occupying the center to plan great undertakings and bequeath boundless blessings for ten thousand generations.

At this time, scorching the great divining tortoise duly confirmed human deliberations. Examining the resulting configuration when the cracks first consumed the ink markings, he found auspicious signs and none of misfortune. The royal capital was indicated beforehand, and his earlier hesitation was resolved. Burning the thornwood brand duly confirmed his own judgment. Inspecting the resulting divinatory figure after boring and piercing the shell, he found favorable signs and none of calamity. The site of the royal domain was confirmed, and his former doubts were settled.

Thereupon, deciding in his royal heart, he occupied this strategically advantageous site in the realm. The ancestral temple and altars were established, the palaces constructed, and the institutions and arrangements shone with new splendor. Here was what the poem calls “the model for the myriad states.” Acting upon his sagacious calculations, he relied upon these natural defenses of the realm. City walls were built, the court and markets established, and the whole undertaking was newly founded in orderly grandeur. Here was what the poem calls “the king of the people below.”

Ah! When King Wu moved to Hao, he insisted upon settling the matter through divine counsel and was thus unwilling to act carelessly. Can we not see here his complete fulfillment of the ruler’s way? It was fitting indeed that the poet praised him. Generally speaking, moving the capital is undertaken for the people; any purpose beyond serving the people is selfish. It is also a means of planning for later generations, and providing for posterity likewise means providing for the people. King Wu moved to Hao because the settlement at Feng could no longer accommodate them; thus he moved solely for the people. That his deliberations concerning the move left nothing unexamined likewise meant that he deliberated for the people. Consider those of later ages: in establishing the capital at Chang’an, they sought only…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
以一面控制諸侯洛陽之遷惟欲以舊迹比隆
周室良非所以爲斯民圖者果可與周武同日
而語哉
念兹皇祖陟降庭止維予小子夙夜敬止
陳器
同考試官教諭何批武王之孝止是箇敬字故
成王欲勉敬以承之詞浮於理者殊爲可厭求其渾厚
爾雅而善寫成王意緒者有如此篇
同考試官教諭戴批官樣題目作者不泛則略
此篇說理精到造語警策殆邃於經學者
同考試官教諭吳批孝敬書生之常談固不
難於操筆詞峻整而思舂容此作得之
考試官教諭林批形容成王追慕之意妙在
紆餘宛轉之中醞藉之學固如是
考試官教授陳批平淡典雅如太羹玄酒
自有深味可錄
表前王克孝之實勉在己持敬之常賢王然也
夫敬之所在即孝之所在也成王表前王之孝
punctuated:
以一面控制諸侯，洛陽之遷惟欲以舊迹比隆周室，良非所以爲斯民圖者，果可與周武同日而語哉？
「念兹皇祖，陟降庭止；維予小子，夙夜敬止。」
陳器
同考試官教諭何批：武王之孝止是箇敬字，故成王欲勉敬以承之。詞浮於理者殊爲可厭，求其渾厚爾雅而善寫成王意緒者，有如此篇。
同考試官教諭戴批：官樣題目，作者不泛則略。此篇說理精到，造語警策，殆邃於經學者。
同考試官教諭吳批：孝敬，書生之常談，固不難於操筆。詞峻整而思舂容，此作得之。
考試官教諭林批：形容成王追慕之意，妙在紆餘宛轉之中，醞藉之學固如是。
考試官教授陳批：平淡典雅，如太羹玄酒，自有深味，可錄。
表前王克孝之實，勉在己持敬之常，賢王然也。夫敬之所在，即孝之所在也。成王表前王之孝
translation_en:
…to control the feudal lords from a single strategic position, while the relocation to Luoyang sought only to rival the glory of the Zhou royal house by occupying its former site. These were certainly not plans made for the people's sake. Can they really be spoken of in the same breath as King Wu of Zhou?
“Mindful of this august ancestor, ascending and descending in the court; I, the little child, remain reverent morning and night.”
Chen Qi
Comment by Associate Examiner He, Instructor: King Wu's filial devotion comes down to the single word “reverence”; hence King Cheng wished to exert himself in reverence so as to carry it forward. Writing whose rhetoric exceeds its reasoning is particularly objectionable. If one seeks a piece that is substantial and refined, and skillfully expresses King Cheng's thoughts and feelings, here is such a work.
Comment by Associate Examiner Dai, Instructor: With a conventional examination topic, writers tend to be either vague or cursory. This piece expounds principles with precision and thoroughness, and its phrasing is incisive and arresting. Its author is surely deeply versed in classical learning.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: Filial devotion and reverence are commonplace subjects among scholars, so taking up the brush to discuss them is certainly not difficult. But this work achieves disciplined, well-ordered expression together with ample, unhurried thought.
Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: The subtlety of this portrayal of King Cheng's yearning for his predecessor lies in its leisurely, winding development. Such is the learning of a cultivated and restrained writer.
Comment by Examiner Chen, Professor: Plain, balanced, and classically elegant, like unseasoned sacrificial broth and “dark wine”—the water offered in sacrifice—it has a profound flavor of its own. Worth selecting.
To manifest the former king's actual achievement of filial devotion, and to strive oneself to sustain constant reverence: this is how a worthy king acts. Wherever reverence resides, filial devotion resides also. King Cheng manifested the former king's filial devotion …

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而自勉以敬其得繼述之道者歟此成王免喪
朝廟而作歎前王永世克孝而勉之以敬蓋謂
昔我皇考之念皇祖痛儀容之永隔而追慕之
心不忘於頃刻惟欲繼其志也念覆育之深恩
而哀慕之情不替於斯須惟欲述其事也心之
所至目常之在皇祖雖遠常若見其陟之于庭
而覩無像於有像恍乎謦欬之有聞念之所切
視之如存皇祖雖往恒若見其降之于庭而視
無形於有形宛乎儀容之相接皇考之克孝如
===
此是皆一敬之所存也顧予小子年甫幼冲負
此守成之託一或不敬則先業隳矣敢自怠乎
眇躬凉薄撫此盈成之運一有不敬則先緒墜
矣敢自畫乎故必夙焉而興虔恭寅畏不以夙
而或懈一以皇考之念皇祖者而念我皇考務
有以踐其遺規也夜焉而寐戰兢惕勵不以夜
而少替一以皇考之思皇祖者而思我皇考務
有以步其後塵也噫成王述前王之考而勉在
巳之敬如此其所以就文武之業而崇大化之
punctuated:
而自勉以敬，其得繼述之道者歟？此成王免喪朝廟而作，歎前王永世克孝，而勉之以敬。蓋謂：「昔我皇考之念皇祖，痛儀容之永隔，而追慕之心不忘於頃刻，惟欲繼其志也；念覆育之深恩，而哀慕之情不替於斯須，惟欲述其事也。心之所至，目常之在，皇祖雖遠，常若見其陟之于庭，而覩無像於有像，恍乎謦欬之有聞；念之所切，視之如存，皇祖雖往，恒若見其降之于庭，而視無形於有形，宛乎儀容之相接。皇考之克孝如此，是皆一敬之所存也。顧予小子，年甫幼冲，負此守成之託，一或不敬，則先業隳矣，敢自怠乎？眇躬凉薄，撫此盈成之運，一有不敬，則先緒墜矣，敢自畫乎？故必夙焉而興，虔恭寅畏，不以夙而或懈，一以皇考之念皇祖者而念我皇考，務有以踐其遺規也；夜焉而寐，戰兢惕勵，不以夜而少替，一以皇考之思皇祖者而思我皇考，務有以步其後塵也。」
噫！成王述前王之考，而勉在巳之敬如此，其所以就文武之業，而崇大化之
translation_en:
…and urges himself to maintain reverence: has he not grasped the way to carry forward his predecessors’ intentions and undertakings? This was composed when King Cheng, having completed mourning, attended the ancestral temple. He praises the former king’s enduring filial devotion and urges himself to reverence. Its meaning is this:
“In former days, when my august late father thought of my august grandfather, he grieved that he was forever separated from his grandfather’s appearance and presence. His longing never left his heart for an instant; his sole desire was to carry forward his intentions. Remembering the profound kindness with which his grandfather had sheltered and nurtured him, his sorrowful affection never diminished for a moment; his sole desire was to carry forward his undertakings. Wherever his heart turned, there his eyes constantly rested [?]. Though my august grandfather was far away, my father always seemed to see him ascending into the court: amid visible images he beheld the imageless, as though he could hear his grandfather clearing his throat. So deeply did he cherish his memory that he regarded him as still present. Though my august grandfather had departed, my father always seemed to see him descending into the court: amid visible forms he perceived the formless, as though encountering his grandfather’s countenance and bearing. Such was my august father’s filial devotion, and it all arose from his unwavering reverence.
“Yet I, his young son, am still of tender years and bear this trust to preserve the accomplishments of my predecessors. Should I fail in reverence even once, their achievements would be ruined. Dare I grow idle? Insignificant and deficient in virtue, I preside over this age of fullness and accomplishment. Should I lapse into irreverence, the legacy of my predecessors would fall. Dare I set limits to my own efforts? Thus I must rise early, devout, respectful, and reverently apprehensive, never allowing the early hour to excuse any slackness. I must think of my august father just as he thought of my august grandfather, striving to put his bequeathed precepts into practice. I must retire late at night, trembling with caution, vigilant and diligent, never allowing the late hour to diminish my effort. I must remember my august father just as he remembered my august grandfather, striving to follow in his footsteps.”
Ah! King Cheng thus recounts the former king’s filial devotion [?; the transcription reads ‘deceased father’] and urges himself to maintain reverence. This was how he brought the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu to fulfillment and exalted the foundation of great transforming influence…

title: 正德八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
本端在此矣抑孝敬者千聖傳心之要致治保
邦之本也故欽明若堯允恭若舜祗德若禹聖
敬若湯乃知自古帝王創業垂統未有不本於
敬也成王有見於此思前王創業之難知在己
守成不易故於嗣大歷服之初拳拳以敬自勉
可謂得聖賢傳心之法嗣王繼述之要也其所
以基命宥密緝熈大業而為有周守成令主夫
豈無自而然哉
春秋
===
宋人圍滕宣公九年宋師伐滕宣公十年
吳榮賀
同考試官教諭李批聖經稱人稱師之意類能
發之明白痛快如此作殊尠當是老於經學者録之
考試官教諭林批以仁義二字發明稱人
稱師之旨良是
考試官教授陳批辭嚴義正春秋文當
如此作
大國始乘難而虐小春秋貶其不仁繼縱惡而
punctuated:
本，端在此矣。抑孝敬者，千聖傳心之要，致治保邦之本也。故欽明若堯，允恭若舜，祗德若禹，聖敬若湯，乃知自古帝王創業垂統，未有不本於敬也。成王有見於此，思前王創業之難，知在己守成不易，故於嗣大歷服之初，拳拳以敬自勉，可謂得聖賢傳心之法、嗣王繼述之要也。其所以基命宥密、緝熈大業，而為有周守成令主，夫豈無自而然哉？

春秋

宋人圍滕，宣公九年；宋師伐滕，宣公十年。

吳榮賀

同考試官教諭李批：聖經稱人稱師之意，類能發之明白痛快，如此作殊尠，當是老於經學者，録之。

考試官教諭林批：以仁義二字發明稱人稱師之旨，良是。

考試官教授陳批：辭嚴義正，春秋文當如此作。

大國始乘難而虐小，春秋貶其不仁；繼縱惡而
translation_en:
…the foundation lies precisely here. Filial devotion and reverence are the essentials of the transmission of the mind among the myriad sages, and the foundation of good government and the preservation of the state. Thus Yao was reverent and enlightened; Shun, truly respectful; Yu, reverent in virtue; and Tang, sagely and reverent. From this we know that, since antiquity, no emperor or king has founded an undertaking and handed down a line of succession without grounding it in reverence. King Cheng understood this. Reflecting on the difficulty with which the former kings had founded their undertaking, he knew that preserving their achievement would be no easy task for him. Thus, from the beginning of his succession to the great imperial charge, he earnestly exhorted himself to reverence. He may be said to have grasped the method by which sages and worthies transmitted the mind, and the essentials by which a succeeding king carries forward his predecessors’ work. Could his establishing the mandate with profound deliberation, continuing and illuminating the great undertaking, and becoming an excellent ruler who preserved Zhou’s achievements possibly have come about without a source?

Spring and Autumn Annals

“Men of Song besieged Teng”—the ninth year of Duke Xuan. “The army of Song attacked Teng”—the tenth year of Duke Xuan.

Wu Ronghe

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: “The meaning of the sage’s classic in using ‘men’ and ‘army’ is generally [?] brought out clearly and forcefully. Compositions such as this are exceedingly rare. The writer must be a seasoned student of the Classics. Accept it.”

Comment by Examiner Lin, Instructor: “Using the two concepts of benevolence and righteousness to elucidate the purport of the terms ‘men’ and ‘army’ is quite right.”

Comment by Examiner Chen, Professor: “The language is stern and the principles correct. Essays on the Spring and Autumn Annals should be written like this.”
